title_en: Sinochem International (Singapore) Co., Ltd. v. ThyssenKrupp Metallurgical Products Co., Ltd. — dispute over an international sales contract
ruling_gist_en: I. Regarding the application of the applicable law. The places of business of the parties in this dispute over an international sale of goods contract were located in Singapore and Germany respectively, and the parties agreed in the contract to apply U.S. law. Singapore, Germany, and the United States are all Contracting States to the United Nations Convention on Contracts for the International Sale of Goods, and the parties did not exclude the application of the Convention. Therefore, the trial of this case shall first apply the United Nations Convention on Contracts for the International Sale of Goods. For issues arising in the case that are not covered by the Convention, such as the validity of the contract and the transfer of ownership, the U.S. law chosen by the parties shall apply.

full_text_en:
Sinochem International (Overseas) Pte Ltd v. ThyssenKrupp Metallurgical Products GmbH — dispute over international sale of goods contract

Ruling Summary

1. Regarding the application of governing law. The parties to this dispute over an international sale of goods contract have their places of business in Singapore and Germany respectively, and the parties agreed in the contract to apply the laws of the United States. Singapore, Germany, and the United States are all Contracting States to the United Nations Convention on Contracts for the International Sale of Goods (CISG). The parties did not exclude the application of the Convention. Therefore, the trial of this case shall first apply the CISG. For issues involved in the trial of the case that are not covered by the Convention, such as the validity of the contract and the transfer of title, the laws of the United States chosen by the parties shall apply.

2. Regarding the determination of fundamental breach under the CISG. In an international sale of goods contract, even if the goods delivered by the seller are defective, as long as the buyer can use the goods or resell them, even at a discount, without unreasonable inconvenience, the quality non-conformity should not be regarded as constituting a fundamental breach within the meaning of the CISG.

Civil Judgment of the Supreme People's Court

(2013) Min Si Zhong Zi No. 35

Appellant (Defendant at First Instance): ThyssenKrupp Metallurgical Products GmbH. Domicile: Hollestr. 7a, 45127 Essen, Germany.

Legal Representatives: Kai-Norman Knoetsch, Managing Director of the company.
Ewald Nelken, Managing Director of the company.

Agents ad litem: Xu Fubin, lawyer of Guangdong Jinghai (Tianjin) Law Firm.
Yan Xinfeng, lawyer of Guangdong Jinghai (Tianjin) Law Firm.

Appellee (Plaintiff at First Instance): Sinochem International (Overseas) Pte Ltd. Domicile: 8 Marina View, No. 34-03 Asia Square Tower 1, Singapore.

Legal Representative: Li Chao, Director of the company.

Agents ad litem: Chen Jinlong, lawyer of Shanghai Hongqiao Zhenghan Law Firm.
Zheng Wei, lawyer of Beijing Tiantong Law Firm.

The Appellant, ThyssenKrupp Metallurgical Products GmbH (hereinafter referred to as ThyssenKrupp Germany), appealed to this Court against the Civil Judgment (2009) Su Min San Chu Zi No. 0004 rendered by the Jiangsu High People's Court (hereinafter referred to as Jiangsu High Court) on December 19, 2012, in the case of the dispute over an international sale of goods contract with the Appellee, Sinochem International (Overseas) Pte Ltd (hereinafter referred to as Sinochem Singapore). This Court formed a collegial panel in accordance with the law and held a public hearing of this case on December 26, 2013. Xu Fubin and Yan Xinfeng, agents ad litem of ThyssenKrupp Germany, and Chen Jinlong and Zheng Wei, agents ad litem of Sinochem Singapore, appeared in court to participate in the proceedings. This case is now concluded.

Sinochem Singapore filed a lawsuit with the court of first instance, the Jiangsu High Court, alleging: On April 11, 2008, Sinochem Singapore and ThyssenKrupp Germany entered into a Purchase Contract, stipulating that Sinochem Singapore would purchase 25,000 metric tons of petroleum coke from ThyssenKrupp Germany, with the HGI index of the petroleum coke to be between 36 and 46. Sinochem Singapore paid the full purchase price as agreed, but the HGI index of the petroleum coke delivered by ThyssenKrupp Germany was only 32, which seriously affected Sinochem Singapore's sales in the Chinese market and constituted a fundamental breach of contract. Sinochem Singapore is entitled to rescind the contract, demand ThyssenKrupp Germany return the full purchase price, and compensate Sinochem Singapore for all losses suffered as a result. Therefore, Sinochem Singapore requested the court to: 1. Rescind the Purchase Contract entered into by the parties; 2. Order ThyssenKrupp Germany to return the purchase price of USD 7,756,828.55 (equivalent to RMB 52,926,392.56 based on the benchmark exchange rate of 6.8232 on May 6, 2009) and interest from September 24, 2008, to the date ThyssenKrupp Germany actually returns the purchase price (calculated according to the同期 USD loan interest rate of Bank of China); 3. Order ThyssenKrupp Germany to compensate Sinochem Singapore for port through-put charges and storage fees of RMB 1,523,052 (provisionally calculated up to May 6, 2009); 4. Order ThyssenKrupp Germany to bear the litigation costs of this case.

ThyssenKrupp Germany argued in its defense: 1. The HGI value of the petroleum coke delivered by ThyssenKrupp Germany was 32. While on the surface this did not conform to the contract, this value was not mandatory. Petroleum coke with an HGI value of 32 does not affect its use, and ThyssenKrupp Germany's actions did not constitute a breach of contract. 2. After the petroleum coke arrived at Nanjing Port, Sinochem Singapore paid the purchase price and did not raise any objections. The reason Sinochem Singapore later raised a quality objection was that the market price of petroleum coke dropped significantly around September and October 2009. 3. Even if ThyssenKrupp Germany constituted a breach of contract, Sinochem Singapore lost its right to claim because it failed to make a claim against ThyssenKrupp Germany within 60 days from the date of arrival of the petroleum coke at the destination port as stipulated in the contract. 4. Sinochem Singapore had already sold the petroleum coke to its parent company, Sinochem International (Holding) Co., Ltd. (hereinafter referred to as Sinochem Holding Company), at a price substantially similar to the price in the subject Purchase Contract, and thus Sinochem Singapore suffered no loss. Therefore, ThyssenKrupp Germany requested the court to: 1. Dismiss Sinochem Singapore's claims; 2. Order Sinochem Singapore to bear the litigation costs of this case.

The Jiangsu High Court found the following upon trial:

I. Facts Agreed Upon by Both Parties

On April 11, 2008, Sinochem Singapore and ThyssenKrupp Germany entered into a Purchase Contract, stipulating: 1. Sinochem Singapore would purchase 25,000 metric tons of fuel-grade petroleum coke from ThyssenKrupp Germany, with a permissible 10% variation in quantity, and the typical HGI index of the petroleum coke was 36-46. 2. The loading port for the petroleum coke was Pittsburgh, California, and the destination port was a Chinese port, the specific port to be determined by Sinochem Singapore. 3. An independent surveyor confirmed by both parties would conduct sampling and testing on board the vessel at the loading port and issue a certificate of analysis, which would be final and binding on both parties. Sinochem Singapore had the right to inspect the quantity and quality of the petroleum coke at the discharge port, and ThyssenKrupp Germany had the right to appoint an independent surveyor to witness the aforementioned inspection process at its own expense. If Sinochem Singapore discovered that the quality or quantity of the petroleum coke did not conform to the quality or quantity determined at the loading port, Sinochem Singapore should send a notice of claim to ThyssenKrupp Germany, and had the right to make a claim against ThyssenKrupp Germany within 60 days from the date of arrival of the petroleum coke at the destination port (Article 7.2.3 of the Purchase Contract). 4. This contract should be governed by, construed, and interpreted in accordance with the laws of the State of New York, United States of America, effective at the time. The parties also made other agreements regarding the performance of the contract.

On August 8, 2008, the certificate of analysis issued by the mutually recognized surveyor, A.J. EDMOND Company, at the loading port indicated that the HGI index of the petroleum coke was 32. The weight certificate issued on August 11, 2008, indicated that ThyssenKrupp Germany actually delivered 26,079.63 metric tons of petroleum coke.

On July 31, 2008, Sinochem Singapore opened a Letter of Credit at the Bank of Communications, Singapore Branch (hereinafter referred to as Singapore BoCom), with Clause 45A specifying: Petroleum coke HGI index CA. 36-46. On August 27, 2008, ThyssenKrupp Germany presented the negotiation documents to Singapore BoCom, including the certificate of analysis issued by A.J. EDMOND Company at the loading port. That bank paid the majority of the purchase price on September 2, 2008. On September 11, 2008, ThyssenKrupp Germany issued a final commercial invoice, determining the unit price of petroleum coke at USD 301.56 per metric ton. On September 25, 2008, Sinochem Singapore paid the remaining small portion of the purchase price via telegraphic transfer. Sinochem Singapore paid a total purchase price of USD 7,756,828.55 to ThyssenKrupp Germany.

On September 8, 2008, the petroleum coke arrived at Nanjing Port. On November 10, 2008, the analysis certificate issued by China Certification & Inspection Group Jiangsu Co., Ltd. indicated that the HGI index of the petroleum coke was 32.

From October to December 2008, the market price of petroleum coke in China fell. The ex-factory price including tax for medium-sulfur coke fell to RMB 2,048 per metric ton in October, fell to RMB 1,357 per metric ton in November, and fell to RMB 1,305 per metric ton in December.

Sinochem Holding Company is the parent company of Sinochem Singapore.

The original name of ThyssenKrupp Germany was ThyssenKrupp Minenergy GmbH, with its domicile at Altendorfer Strasse 120, D-45143 Essen, Germany. On June 24, 2011, it changed its name to ThyssenKrupp Metallurgical Products GmbH, and its domicile changed to Hollestr. 7a, 45127 Essen, Germany.

II. The Parties' Positions on Whether the HGI Index of the Subject Petroleum Coke Conformed to the Contract

Sinochem Singapore argued that the HGI index of the petroleum coke delivered by ThyssenKrupp Germany was 32, which did not conform to the contract, was difficult to sell in the Chinese market, and constituted a fundamental breach. To support its position, Sinochem Singapore provided an "Explanation on the Characteristics of Petroleum Coke" issued by the School of Materials Science and Engineering, Shanghai University. This explanation stated: The hardness (HGI index) of fuel-grade petroleum coke is a core indicator. Typically, large enterprises require the hardness index of purchased fuel-grade petroleum coke to be no less than 45. Where the mill type permits, some enterprises also accept petroleum coke with a hardness index above 35. The uses for fuel-grade petroleum coke with a hardness index below 35 are very limited. Therefore, such demand is rare in the domestic fuel-grade petroleum coke market. ThyssenKrupp Germany argued that this evidence constituted witness testimony, and the witness did not appear in court to testify, so it did not confirm its authenticity.

ThyssenKrupp Germany argued that although the HGI index of the petroleum coke it delivered was 32, which on the surface did not conform to the contract, it did not actually constitute a breach. The HGI index stipulated in the contract was a typical value. Petroleum coke with an HGI index of 32 could still be sold in the Chinese market. To support its position, ThyssenKrupp Germany applied for three expert witnesses to testify in court: Mr. Fisher, an American with over thirty years of experience in the petroleum coke industry; Mr. Wang Pingfu, former Vice President of the Zhengzhou Light Metals Research Institute of CHALCO; and Professor Li Yonghua from North China Electric Power University. These three expert witnesses unanimously agreed: The HGI index indicates the grindability index of petroleum coke. The lower the index, the harder the petroleum coke and the more difficult the grinding. The higher the index, the softer the petroleum coke and the easier the grinding. Petroleum coke with an HGI index of 32 has use value and meets the purpose of the subject Purchase Contract. Additionally, Mr. Fisher stated that the lowest HGI index he had ever seen was 35, and the highest was 85. It is difficult to accurately determine the HGI index of petroleum coke, and it is usually expressed as a range of typical values. Mr. Wang Pingfu stated that for harder petroleum coke, it is necessary to adjust grinding parameters such as the mill feed rate, air pressure and flow rate, and mill speed before use. Mr. Li Yonghua stated that the HGI index is the basis for selecting the fuel pulverizing system and cannot be used as a criterion for judging whether it is a fuel. Petroleum coke with a lower HGI index requires replacement of grinding equipment before it can be used.

Sinochem Singapore did not object to the authenticity of the testimony of ThyssenKrupp Germany's witnesses but emphasized that Mr. Fisher's testimony indicated that in his thirty-year professional career, he had never seen petroleum coke with an HGI index of 32; the lowest HGI index he had seen was 35. Mr. Wang Pingfu himself had not performed HGI index testing or used petroleum coke with different HGI indexes, so the authority of his testimony was questionable. Mr. Li Yonghua's testimony indicated that petroleum coke with different HGI indexes requires different grinding equipment, and petroleum coke with a higher hardness (lower HGI index) requires equipment replacement before use.

The Jiangsu High Court held that regarding the parts of the testimony of the three expert witnesses provided by ThyssenKrupp Germany concerning the relationship between the HGI index and hardness of petroleum coke and the use value of the subject petroleum coke with an HGI index of 32, the testimonies corroborated each other, had a scientific basis, and could be admitted. Regarding whether petroleum coke with an HGI index of 32 met the purpose of the contract, this was a matter for adjudication, and the witnesses had no authority to make such a judgment. Therefore, the court did not admit the parts of the three expert testimonies concerning the conformity of the subject petroleum coke with an HGI index of 32 to the contract purpose. The court would provide a detailed analysis of whether the subject petroleum coke with an HGI index of 32 met the contract purpose in the Judgment Reasoning section. The "Explanation on the Characteristics of Petroleum Coke" provided by Sinochem Singapore was not issued in an individual capacity but in the name of the School of Materials Science and Engineering, Shanghai University, and bore the official seal of the institution. Its content did not deny that petroleum coke with an HGI index of 32 could be used, but merely stated that its uses were limited. The content of this explanation could, to a certain extent, corroborate the testimony of the three expert witnesses provided by ThyssenKrupp Germany, had a scientific basis, and could be admitted.

Furthermore, ThyssenKrupp Germany also provided a Quality Inspection Certificate issued by China Certification & Inspection Group Beijing Co., Ltd., intended to prove that the HGI index of the delivered petroleum coke was 36. Sinochem Singapore did not recognize the authenticity, legality, or relevance of this evidence, arguing that: 1. After the subject petroleum coke arrived at the destination port, it was always under Sinochem Singapore's control, and ThyssenKrupp Germany did not take samples of the subject petroleum coke from Sinochem Singapore for inspection. Therefore, the petroleum coke sample used by ThyssenKrupp Germany for testing was not the subject petroleum coke. 2. ThyssenKrupp Germany unilaterally commissioned China Certification & Inspection Group Beijing Co., Ltd. to conduct the inspection without Sinochem Singapore's consent, which lacked contractual and legal basis. The Jiangsu High Court held that since it could not be determined whether the petroleum coke sample used by ThyssenKrupp Germany for testing was taken from the subject petroleum coke, and its unilateral commission of inspection lacked contractual basis, the relevance and legality of this evidence were not confirmed.

III. Facts Regarding Communications Between the Parties Concerning the HGI Index of the Subject Petroleum Coke

On October 15, 2008, Sinochem Holding Company sent a letter to ThyssenKrupp Germany, stating that the HGI index of the delivered subject petroleum coke seriously deviated from the contractually agreed range, the end users could not use it and refused to take delivery, the situation was serious, and requested ThyssenKrupp Germany to propose a solution as soon as possible. During its first oral argument at the trial of first instance, ThyssenKrupp Germany recognized that Sinochem Holding Company's actions represented Sinochem Singapore. On November 4, 2008, Sinochem Singapore sent another letter to ThyssenKrupp Germany, stating that the HGI index of the petroleum coke delivered by ThyssenKrupp Germany seriously deviated from the contractually agreed range, constituting a material breach, and requesting ThyssenKrupp Germany to properly address the matter. On November 12, 2008, ThyssenKrupp Germany replied to Sinochem Singapore, stating that the HGI index of the delivered petroleum coke was only slightly below the range stipulated in the Purchase Contract, did not constitute a material breach, and agreed to hold meetings to discuss a solution. On November 27, 2008, Sinochem Singapore sent a letter to ThyssenKrupp Germany requesting an early meeting between the parties. On December 8, 2008, ThyssenKrupp Germany replied to Sinochem Singapore, stating that a meeting before the end of 2008 would be difficult and suggesting a meeting in January 2009.

The above facts are evidenced by the fax sent by Sinochem Holding Company to ThyssenKrupp Germany on October 15, 2008, the letters sent to ThyssenKrupp Germany on November 4 and November 27, 2008, provided by Sinochem Singapore, and the replies from ThyssenKrupp Germany dated November 12 and December 8, 2008. ThyssenKrupp Germany had no objection to the authenticity of the above evidence. The Jiangsu High Court confirmed the facts regarding the communications between the parties concerning the HGI index of the subject petroleum coke.

Sinochem Singapore stated that, in addition to written correspondence, it also had several oral communications with ThyssenKrupp Germany. ThyssenKrupp Germany disputed this. Sinochem Singapore did not provide any related evidence to prove it.

IV. Disposition of the Subject Petroleum Coke

During the trial of this case, to avoid further losses caused by the prolonged storage of the disputed petroleum coke at Nanjing Port, Sinochem Singapore sent a letter to Krupp Germany on November 11, 2009, informing it of the price preliminarily negotiated with a potential buyer and other information, and solicited Krupp Germany's opinion. On November 18, 2009, Krupp Germany replied by letter, asserting that it had fulfilled its delivery obligation, that Sinochem Singapore did not need to consult it, much less obtain its consent, regarding the disposal of the disputed petroleum coke, and that it could not provide any comment on the price proposed by Sinochem Singapore. On November 26, 2009, Sinochem Singapore commissioned Sinochem Holding Company to enter into a sales contract with Weihai Jinho Import & Export Trade Co., Ltd. (hereinafter referred to as Jinho Company) to sell the disputed petroleum coke at RMB 1,575.50 per ton. Sinochem Singapore recovered RMB 34,637,187.25 (converted at exchange rates of 6.8284 and 6.8283 respectively, equivalent to USD 5,072,525.65) from the disposal of the disputed petroleum coke. In the process of selling the disputed petroleum coke, Sinochem Singapore incurred the following additional expenses: (1) taxes and fees of RMB 1,600,255.71 (converted at an exchange rate of 6.8359, equivalent to USD 234,095.83); (2) lump-sum fees of RMB 834,549 (converted at an exchange rate of 6.8309, equivalent to USD 122,172.63); (3) storage fees of RMB 1,120,000 (converted at an exchange rate of 6.8263, equivalent to USD 164,071.31); (4) inspection fees of RMB 10,000 (converted at an exchange rate of 6.8317, equivalent to USD 1,463.76); (5) customs declaration fees of RMB 27,029.36 (converted at an exchange rate of 6.8261, equivalent to USD 3,959.71); (6) financial expenses of USD 2,490. The total additional expenses incurred by Sinochem Singapore in the process of selling the disputed petroleum coke amounted to USD 528,253.24.

The above facts are evidenced by: the letter from Sinochem Singapore dated November 11, 2009 regarding the timely reduction of losses by disposing of the disputed petroleum coke; the reply letter from Krupp Germany's lawyer dated November 18, 2009; the letter entrusting the sale of the disputed petroleum coke; the sales contract dated November 26, 2009; five invoices dated December 17-30, 2009; charts of crude oil and petroleum coke price trends; five invoices; special receipts for customs deposits, risk guarantees, and collateral; the import tariff schedule; the special payment form for import duties at Nanjing Xinshengwei Customs; payment documents and invoices for inspection fees; payment documents and invoices for customs declaration fees; and the port storage and agency contract. Krupp Germany raised no objection to the authenticity of the other evidence, except for arguing that the letter entrusting the sale of the disputed petroleum coke had not been notarized and apostilled. The Jiangsu High People's Court held that Sinochem Holding Company and Sinochem Singapore are parent and subsidiary companies, and the letter entrusting the sale of the disputed petroleum coke was obtained domestically in China and did not require notarization or apostille; the authenticity of this evidence could be confirmed. Therefore, the Jiangsu High People's Court confirmed the above facts.

V. Regarding the Losses of Sinochem Singapore

Krupp Germany argued that Sinochem Singapore had sold the disputed petroleum coke at the original price to its parent company, Sinochem Holding Company, and therefore suffered no loss. Sinochem Singapore acknowledged the existence of a sales contract for petroleum coke between itself and Sinochem Holding Company at a price substantially similar to that of the procurement contract, but contended that the relationship between them was not a genuine sale but a consignment for sale. Sinochem Singapore stated that its purpose in purchasing the disputed petroleum coke from Krupp Germany was to sell it within China, and the sales contract between Sinochem Singapore and Sinochem Holding Company was executed for customs declaration purposes, to facilitate the smooth entry of the disputed petroleum coke into China and to enable Sinochem Holding Company to act as its agent for domestic sales. To support its claim, Sinochem Singapore submitted a letter of authorization entrusting Sinochem Holding Company to sell the disputed petroleum coke. Krupp Germany did not dispute the formal authenticity of this letter but suspected that it had been backdated for the purpose of claiming damages in this case. The Jiangsu High People's Court held that the letter of authorization provided by Sinochem Singapore was an original document, and in the absence of contrary evidence, it could be admitted.

Sinochem Singapore argued that the amount of payment it made to Krupp Germany was USD 7,756,828.55. After deducting the proceeds of USD 5,072,525.65 recovered from the disposal of the disputed petroleum coke, Krupp Germany should return USD 2,684,302.9 to Sinochem Singapore, plus interest calculated from September 25, 2008 until the date of actual repayment at the lending rate for US dollars of the Bank of China for the corresponding period. Krupp Germany contended that the price difference loss suffered by Sinochem Singapore was caused by the decline in the petroleum coke market, not by the fact that the HGI index of the disputed petroleum coke did not conform to the procurement contract. Such loss was a normal commercial risk that should be borne by Sinochem Singapore.

In addition, Sinochem Singapore also demanded compensation from Krupp Germany for the following additional expenses incurred in disposing of the disputed petroleum coke: taxes and fees of USD 234,095.83, lump-sum fees of USD 122,172.63, and storage fees of USD 164,071.31, totaling USD 520,339.77. As for the inspection fees, customs declaration fees, and financial expenses, Sinochem Singapore expressly stated that it did not seek compensation from Krupp Germany. Krupp Germany argued that its actions did not constitute a breach of contract, and that these expenses were costs that Sinochem Singapore should have borne in reselling the disputed petroleum coke and should not be borne by Krupp Germany.

The Jiangsu High People's Court held as follows:

I. Regarding the Application of Law to This Case

Sinochem Singapore is a Singaporean company, and Krupp Germany is a German company; therefore, this case is a dispute over an international sales contract for petroleum coke. Although the parties stipulated in the contract that the contract should be entered into, governed, and interpreted in accordance with the laws of the State of New York, USA, in force at the time, both parties in the litigation chose the United Nations Convention on Contracts for the International Sale of Goods (hereinafter referred to as the CISG) as the basis for determining their rights and obligations. Since both Singapore and Germany are contracting states to the CISG, the relevant provisions of the CISG shall apply to the contract in dispute.

II. Krupp Germany's Conduct Constituted a Fundamental Breach of Contract

The parties expressly stipulated in the sales contract that the typical HGI index of the disputed petroleum coke ranged between 36 and 46. The inspector recognized by both parties tested the HGI index of the disputed petroleum coke at the port of loading and found it to be 32. The re-inspection conducted by Sinochem Singapore at the port of destination in accordance with the terms of the Procurement Contract also showed that the HGI index of the disputed petroleum coke was 32. On this basis, Sinochem Singapore argued that the HGI index of the disputed petroleum coke was far lower than the standard stipulated in the sales contract and also lower than the quality of general petroleum coke sold domestically, making it difficult to sell in the domestic market and frustrating the intended purpose of the contract at the time of its formation. Therefore, Krupp Germany's conduct constituted a fundamental breach of contract. Krupp Germany argued that the HGI index stipulated in the sales contract was a typical value, not a mandatory indicator, but merely an approximate range; the contract did not set a minimum or maximum range for the HGI index of the disputed petroleum coke, and exceeding that range constituted neither a fundamental breach nor even a general breach. In response to Krupp Germany's argument, Sinochem Singapore countered that the reason the parties did not stipulate an exact value for the HGI index of the petroleum coke but rather a range of typical values was precisely due to the uncertainty of the HGI index. The uncertainty of the HGI index does not mean that the agreed range of typical values is not binding. On this point, the Jiangsu High People's Court held that since the parties stipulated in the Procurement Contract that the typical HGI index of the disputed petroleum coke ranged between 36 and 46, this means that the typical HGI index of the petroleum coke delivered by Krupp Germany should not be lower than 36 or higher than 46; exceeding this range constitutes a breach of contract. Krupp Germany's argument that the parties did not set a minimum or maximum range for the typical HGI index of the disputed petroleum coke in the Procurement Contract and that the stipulated range of typical HGI indices is not a mandatory indicator and is not binding was unfounded and was not supported by the court. The Jiangsu High People's Court held that since the Procurement Contract stipulated that the HGI index of the petroleum coke was a typical value, the test should determine the typical HGI index of the disputed petroleum coke. After two inspections at the port of loading and the port of destination, the typical HGI index of the petroleum coke actually delivered by Krupp Germany was 32 in both cases, which was lower than the minimum of the agreed typical HGI index range. Accordingly, the court determined that the HGI index of the petroleum coke delivered by Krupp Germany did not conform to the contract and constituted a breach of contract.

Sinochem Singapore argued that, as a trader, its purpose in purchasing the disputed petroleum coke was to sell it within China. The fact that the HGI index of the petroleum coke delivered by Krupp Germany did not conform to the contract prevented Sinochem Singapore from selling it normally in China, ultimately depriving it of its expected benefits, and thus constituted a fundamental breach of contract. Krupp Germany argued that the opinions of its three expert witnesses and the fact that Sinochem Singapore resold the disputed petroleum coke to Jinho Company all demonstrated that petroleum coke with an HGI index of 32 could actually be used domestically. The Jiangsu High People's Court held that both parties agreed that the HGI index indicates the hardness of petroleum coke: the higher the index, the lower the hardness; the lower the index, the higher the hardness. This indicates that the HGI index has a significant impact on the hardness of petroleum coke. Mr. Fisher, an expert witness for Krupp Germany and a professional with long-term experience in the petroleum coke industry, testified in court that the lowest HGI index he had encountered in his career was 35. Mr. Fisher's testimony showed that petroleum coke with an HGI index of 32 is indeed extremely rare, or that the deviation of the HGI index of the disputed petroleum coke from the range agreed in the contract was quite severe. Mr. Li Yonghua, another expert witness for Krupp Germany, testified in court that the HGI index is the basis for selecting the fuel pulverizing system, and petroleum coke with a low HGI index and high hardness requires replacement of equipment before it can be used. This indicates that petroleum coke with different HGI indices has different requirements for grinding equipment. Petroleum coke with an HGI index as low as 32 necessarily imposes special requirements on grinding equipment, which means that the market demand for such petroleum coke is extremely limited. Therefore, the delivery by Krupp Germany of petroleum coke with an HGI index as low as 32 to Sinochem Singapore inevitably created great difficulties for Sinochem Singapore's sales, effectively depriving Sinochem Singapore of the benefits it expected to obtain from entering into the Procurement Contract. As a professional company engaged in the petroleum coke trade, Krupp Germany could not have been unaware of the losses its breach of contract might cause to Sinochem Singapore. Accordingly, the Jiangsu High People's Court determined that Krupp Germany's conduct constituted a fundamental breach of contract.

III. Sinochem Singapore Is Entitled to Declare the Contract Avoided

Sinochem Singapore requested the court to order the rescission of the contract on the ground that Krupp Germany had fundamentally breached the contract, which should be understood as a request for the court to declare the contract avoided in accordance with the provisions of the CISG. Krupp Germany argued that, according to Article 49(1)(a) and Article 49(2)(b)(i) of the CISG, where the seller has already delivered the goods, the buyer, if it wishes to declare the contract avoided on the ground that the seller's delivery of goods non-conforming to the contract constitutes a fundamental breach, must do so within a reasonable time after it knew or ought to have known of the fundamental breach. Sinochem Singapore failed to issue a notice of avoidance within a reasonable time and thus lost its right to declare the contract avoided. The Jiangsu High People's Court held that Krupp Germany's argument was untenable. The reasons are as follows:

Article 39(1) of the CISG provides that the buyer loses the right to rely on a lack of conformity of the goods if it does not give notice to the seller specifying the nature of the lack of conformity within a reasonable time after it has discovered it or ought to have discovered it. Article 40 provides that the seller is not entitled to rely on the provisions of Article 39 if the lack of conformity relates to facts of which the seller knew or could not have been unaware and which it did not disclose to the buyer. Although, on its face, this provision applies to general breaches, by analogy, the principle that the greater includes the lesser (argumentum a fortiori) means that this provision also applies to the declaration of avoidance of contract due to fundamental breach caused by a serious lack of conformity in delivery. In this case, Krupp Germany knew at the port of loading that the HGI index of the petroleum coke it delivered was 32, seriously deviating from the agreed specifications. It neither informed Sinochem Singapore of this fact before shipment nor asked Sinochem Singapore whether it was willing to accept petroleum coke with an HGI index of 32; instead, it directly shipped the goods to Sinochem Singapore. Under these circumstances, Krupp Germany is not entitled to argue that Sinochem Singapore lost its right to declare the contract avoided on the ground that Sinochem Singapore failed to issue a notice of avoidance within a reasonable time.

In fact, Sinochem Singapore's declaration of avoidance did not exceed a reasonable period. After the petroleum coke arrived at the port of destination on September 8, 2008, and Sinochem Singapore discovered the HGI index was 32, in accordance with Article 7.2.3 of the Procurement Contract, on October 15 of the same year, it sent a letter to Krupp Germany stating that the HGI index of the delivered petroleum coke seriously deviated from the contractually agreed range, that end users were unable to use it, that it refused to take delivery, that the situation was serious, and requesting Krupp Germany to provide a handling opinion as soon as possible. To further verify the quality of the petroleum coke, Sinochem Singapore conducted a re-inspection. The re-inspection results showed that the HGI index of the disputed petroleum coke was 32, not conforming to the contract. Subsequently, Sinochem Singapore sent multiple letters to Krupp Germany, stating that the HGI index of the petroleum coke delivered by Krupp Germany seriously deviated from the contractually agreed range, constituting a fundamental breach, and requesting proper resolution of the quality issue of the petroleum coke. However, due to Krupp Germany's lack of cooperation, the matter was not resolved. The Jiangsu High People's Court held that after discovering that the HGI index of the disputed petroleum coke seriously deviated from the contract, Sinochem Singapore promptly communicated with Krupp Germany and, failing a resolution, initiated litigation to seek avoidance of the contract. This should be regarded as Sinochem Singapore having issued a notice of avoidance to Krupp Germany within a reasonable time after it knew or ought to have known of the fundamental breach, in compliance with Article 26 of the CISG. Krupp Germany's argument that Sinochem Singapore failed to issue a notice of avoidance within a reasonable time and thus lost its right to declare the contract avoided was unfounded and was not supported by the Jiangsu High People's Court.

Krupp Germany further argued that Sinochem Singapore had already sold the disputed petroleum coke to Jinho Company in November 2009 and could no longer return the goods in substantially the same condition as it had received them. According to Article 82(1) of the CISG, Sinochem Singapore had lost its right to declare the contract avoided. The Jiangsu High People's Court held that after Sinochem Singapore discovered that Krupp Germany's delivery constituted a fundamental breach, it immediately contacted Krupp Germany, but Krupp Germany failed to cooperate, forcing Sinochem Singapore to file a lawsuit. During the trial, to avoid further losses, Sinochem Singapore again discussed the proper disposal of the disputed petroleum coke with Krupp Germany, but Krupp Germany expressly refused. Sinochem Singapore had no choice but to sell the disputed petroleum coke to Jinho Company. Therefore, the responsibility for the inability to return the disputed petroleum coke to Krupp Germany in the same condition as received lies with Krupp Germany, not with Sinochem Singapore. Pursuant to Article 82(2)(a) of the CISG, Sinochem Singapore had not lost its right to declare the contract avoided.

In addition, Krupp Germany argued that Sinochem Singapore had paid the full purchase price, and that this act indicated that Sinochem Singapore was satisfied with the quality of the petroleum coke and had accepted the disputed petroleum coke, and therefore it was no longer entitled to raise objections to the quality of the petroleum coke. The Jiangsu High People's Court held that, according to the terms of the Procurement Contract, Sinochem Singapore's right to raise objections to the quality of the petroleum coke and seek remedies was limited to a period of 60 days after the arrival of the goods at the port, and that this right was unrelated to whether Sinochem Singapore had paid the purchase price. This means that even if Sinochem Singapore had paid the purchase price, as long as it did not exceed 60 days after the arrival of the goods at the port, Sinochem Singapore still had the right to raise objections to the quality of the petroleum coke and seek remedies. Krupp Germany's argument that Sinochem Singapore's payment of the full purchase price should be regarded as its satisfaction with the quality of the disputed petroleum coke and acceptance of the goods, thereby losing its right to raise objections to the quality of the disputed petroleum coke and seek remedies, was unfounded and was not supported by the Jiangsu High People's Court.

IV. Liability of Krupp Germany

Pursuant to Articles 74, 77, 81, and 84 of the CISG, after declaring the contract avoided, Sinochem Singapore is entitled to request Krupp Germany to return the purchase price already paid, plus interest from the date of receipt of the purchase price, and to compensate Sinochem Singapore for the economic losses it suffered as a result of Krupp Germany's breach of contract. In this case, the amount of the purchase price paid by Sinochem Singapore to Krupp Germany was USD 7,756,828.55. To mitigate the losses caused by Krupp Germany's breach of contract, Sinochem Singapore disposed of the disputed petroleum coke and recovered proceeds of USD 5,072,525.65. After deducting this amount, Krupp Germany should return USD 2,684,302.9 to Sinochem Singapore, plus interest on this amount from the date of payment by Sinochem Singapore (September 25, 2008) until the date of actual repayment. Sinochem Singapore incurred additional expenses of USD 528,253.24 in the process of disposing of the disputed petroleum coke. These expenses constitute losses suffered by Sinochem Singapore as a result of Krupp Germany's breach of contract. Sinochem Singapore only seeks compensation from Krupp Germany in the amount of USD 520,339.77, which should be upheld.

Krupp argued that Sinochem Singapore had not suffered any loss because it had already sold the petroleum coke in question to its parent company, Sinochem Holding Company, at the original price. The Jiangsu High People's Court found that this argument of Krupp could not be sustained. Sinochem Singapore stated that it had entered into the sales contract with Sinochem Holding Company solely for customs clearance purposes, to facilitate the smooth entry of the petroleum coke into China and to authorize Sinochem Holding Company to sell the goods on its behalf within China. It claimed that the relationship between them was not a genuine sales relationship but a consignment sales relationship, and it submitted the consignment sales contract as evidence. On October 15, 2008, it was Sinochem Holding Company that, on behalf of Sinochem Singapore, communicated with Krupp regarding the HGI index of the petroleum coke, and Krupp raised no objection. Subsequently, Sinochem Singapore also communicated with Krupp many times regarding the HGI index of the petroleum coke, and Krupp never argued that Sinochem Singapore had already resold the petroleum coke to Sinochem Holding Company and thus had no right to raise objections about the HGI index. This shows that Krupp was well aware of the consignment sales relationship between Sinochem Singapore and Sinochem Holding Company. During the course of this litigation, Sinochem Singapore also entrusted Sinochem Holding Company to sell the petroleum coke on its behalf in order to mitigate losses. This further corroborates Sinochem Singapore's claim that its relationship with Sinochem Holding Company was one of consignment sales, not a sales contract. Based on this, the Jiangsu High People's Court determined that the relationship between Sinochem Singapore and Sinochem Holding Company was a consignment sales relationship, not a sales contract. Krupp's argument that Sinochem Singapore had already sold the petroleum coke to Sinochem Holding Company at the original contract price and thus suffered no loss was without basis and was not supported by the Jiangsu High People's Court.

Krupp also argued that Sinochem Singapore's losses were caused by the decline in the price of petroleum coke, for which it should not bear liability. The Jiangsu High People's Court held that the reason for declaring the subject Procurement Contract avoided was Krupp's fundamental breach of contract, not the market price decline. If the HGI index of the petroleum coke delivered by Krupp had complied with the contractual specifications, Sinochem Singapore would not have been entitled to declare the contract avoided on grounds of price decline, even if prices had fallen; in that case, the price decline would have been a commercial risk to be borne by Sinochem Singapore. Where the subject Procurement Contract was declared avoided due to Krupp's fundamental breach, the risk of price decline falls on Krupp as a commercial risk. Therefore, in this case, even if losses resulted from changes in the petroleum coke market, they should be borne by Krupp.

In summary, the HGI index of the petroleum coke delivered by Krupp seriously deviated from the specifications in the subject Procurement Contract, constituting a fundamental breach, and Krupp must bear the consequences of the declaration of avoidance of the contract. The Jiangsu High People's Court, pursuant to Articles 25, 26, 39(1), 40, 49(1)(a) and 49(2)(b)(i), 74, 77, 81, 82(1) and 82(2)(a), 84 of the CISG, and Article 128 of the Civil Procedure Law of the People's Republic of China, rendered the following judgment: (1) The Procurement Contract entered into between Krupp and Sinochem Singapore on April 11, 2008, is declared avoided. (2) Krupp shall, within thirty days from the effective date of this judgment, return to Sinochem Singapore the payment of USD 2,684,302.9 and pay interest from September 25, 2008 to the date of actual payment as determined in this judgment (calculated at the U.S. dollar lending rate of the Bank of China for the corresponding period). (3) Krupp shall, within thirty days from the effective date of this judgment, compensate Sinochem Singapore for losses in the amount of USD 520,339.77. If Krupp fails to perform the above payment obligations within the period specified in this judgment, it shall pay double the interest on the debt for the period of delayed performance in accordance with Article 229 of the Civil Procedure Law of the People's Republic of China. The case acceptance fee of RMB 306,432 shall be borne by Krupp.

Krupp, dissatisfied with the first-instance judgment of the Jiangsu High People's Court, appealed to this Court, arguing: First, the first-instance judgment erred in its determination of the applicable law. According to the contract and China's conflict of laws rules, the law of the State of New York, USA, should apply to this case. The CISG should apply to this case, and the interpretation of the CISG, the Uniform Commercial Code of the United States, and commercial practices should also apply. The "Digest of Case Law on the United Nations Convention on Contracts for the International Sale of Goods" should also be the basis for adjudicating this case. The Jiangsu High People's Court was wrong to hold that only the CISG applies. Second, the Jiangsu High People's Court erroneously found that Sinochem Singapore and Sinochem Holding Company had an agency relationship. The relationship was a sales contract; Sinochem Singapore, having successfully resold the goods, had no right to assert the claims in this case. Third, the first-instance judgment erroneously found that Krupp's delivery of petroleum coke with an HGI index of 32 constituted a fundamental breach. (1) Krupp's delivery of petroleum coke with an HGI index of 32 did not constitute a mere breach. The HGI index was not a mandatory indicator but only an approximate range. The contract did not provide for price adjustments for such a non-essential indicator as the HGI value. Considering the conduct of the contracting parties, a reasonable buyer who believed that an HGI value of 32 was non-conforming and constituted a fundamental breach would not have raised objections about the quality of the goods two months after receiving the inspection certificate, or even after taking delivery and paying the full price. (2) Krupp's delivery of petroleum coke with an HGI index of 32 did not constitute a fundamental breach. Although the HGI value was low, the petroleum coke still had its intended use value and commercial value. Moreover, Sinochem Singapore resold the goods in November 2009 at a price higher than the prevailing market price. Thus, the petroleum coke with an HGI index of 32 did not fundamentally deprive Sinochem Singapore of what it was entitled to under the contract, nor did it frustrate its contractual purpose. The Jiangsu High People's Court's finding that Krupp's breach was fundamental was factually incorrect and lacked legal basis. Fourth, Sinochem Singapore failed to give notice of avoidance within a reasonable time and has lost its right to declare the contract avoided. Declaring the contract avoided several months after learning of the HGI index of 32, and in the context of a significant market downturn, cannot be considered as having been done within a reasonable time. The Jiangsu High People's Court's determination of the reasonable time seriously violated the relevant provisions and legislative intent of the CISG. Fifth, even if Krupp's delivery of petroleum coke with an HGI index of 32 constituted a mere breach, Sinochem Singapore, having failed to raise a quality objection within a reasonable time, has lost its right to claim non-conformity. Sixth, the first-instance judgment seriously erred in determining the amount of loss. Under Article 76 of the CISG, assuming Sinochem Singapore was entitled to declare the contract avoided, damages should be calculated based on the difference between the contract price and the price at the time Sinochem Singapore took over the goods. However, the first-instance judgment erroneously calculated damages based on the difference between the contract price and the price at which the goods were resold to Jinhou Company in November 2009, which clearly contradicts the CISG. Seventh, Sinochem Singapore's claim in the first instance was to request the court to rescind the Procurement Contract between the parties, and it never requested the court to declare the Procurement Contract avoided. The Jiangsu High People's Court sua sponte declared the contract avoided, exceeding the scope of the claim, in violation of the law. In conclusion, Krupp requested: (1) that the judgment be reversed and all of Sinochem Singapore's claims be dismissed; (2) that Sinochem Singapore be ordered to bear all litigation costs of the first and second instances.

Sinochem Singapore responded: First, the first-instance judgment correctly applied the CISG based on the choice of both parties. According to the parties' agreement in the Procurement Contract, the law of the State of New York, USA, should apply, and Krupp argued that the CISG is part of the law of New York. However, the "Digest of Case Law on the United Nations Convention on Contracts for the International Sale of Goods" is not part of the CISG nor an official interpretation of the Convention, and cannot serve as the legal basis for this case. Second, Sinochem Singapore entrusted Sinochem Holding Company to sell the petroleum coke on its behalf; the relationship between them was one of consignment, not sales. The first-instance judgment correctly found this. Sinochem Singapore's entrustment of Sinochem Holding Company to sell the petroleum coke was acknowledged by Krupp. After the petroleum coke arrived at Nanjing Port, Sinochem Holding Company, as Sinochem Singapore's agent, directly contacted Krupp, and Krupp recognized its agent status. Krupp's subsequent objection to Sinochem Holding Company's status as a consignee in this litigation violates the principle of promissory estoppel. Third, the HGI index of the petroleum coke was a key quality indicator expressly agreed upon by both parties. Krupp delivered petroleum coke with an HGI value of 32, which was severely below the contractual specification, causing great difficulty for Sinochem Singapore in reselling the goods, frustrating the purpose of the contract, and constituting a fundamental breach. Sinochem Singapore's payment to Krupp cannot be construed as acceptance of non-conforming goods. Under the contract, quality objections could be raised within 60 days after the petroleum coke arrived at the destination port. Fourth, under the CISG, Krupp, having failed to disclose the non-conformity of the goods, is not entitled to raise a "reasonable time" defense. Moreover, Sinochem Singapore initiated the dispute resolution mechanism agreed upon by the parties within a reasonable time and asserted to Krupp that the goods were non-conforming and constituted a fundamental breach. The first-instance judgment correctly found that Sinochem Singapore's declaration of avoidance was not made beyond a reasonable time. Fifth, the first-instance judgment correctly determined Sinochem Singapore's losses. Sinochem Singapore claimed losses under Article 74 of the CISG, but Krupp erroneously misinterpreted and invoked Article 76, which has no basis. The total amount of losses claimed by Sinochem Singapore represents the actual losses it suffered and does not change depending on the time at which the market price is calculated. Sixth, "declaration of avoidance" under the CISG has the same connotation as "rescission of contract" under Chinese law. In this case, there was no issue of the court exceeding the scope of the claim. In conclusion, the first-instance judgment had clear findings of fact and correct application of law. Sinochem Singapore requested that Krupp's appeal be dismissed.

The facts found by the Jiangsu High People's Court in the first instance were supported by relevant evidence, and the parties raised no objections. This Court confirms those facts.

This Court additionally finds: In a letter dated November 11, 2009, from Sinochem Singapore to Krupp regarding handling the disputed goods to reduce losses in a timely manner, it stated: "Since your company refuses to sign a loss-stopping agreement with us, in order to reduce the losses arising from the disputed goods and to protect the common rights of both parties, we have found a buyer for the disputed goods, and through our agent, Sinochem International (Holding) Co., Ltd., we have preliminarily agreed with the potential buyer on price and other matters, i.e., the settlement quantity is 25,722.339 metric tons (the same pile of imported petroleum coke from the vessel BALTIC FRONTIER, transferred without re-sorting), unit price RMB 1,575.50 per metric ton, ex-hold at Nanjing Huining Wharf, which is not below the reasonable market price." During the second instance, Krupp submitted the Uniform Commercial Code of the United States and relevant cases [Lomaglio Assocs. v. LBK Mktg. Corp., 1999 U.S. Dist. LEXIS 14185 (S.D.N.Y. 1999)], arguing that according to U.S. law, the contract was validly formed and effective.

Sinochem Singapore did not object to the U.S. law submitted by Krupp but argued that the law should be explained by a professional qualified to practice U.S. law and did not recognize the explanation provided by Krupp's agent ad litem. Sinochem Singapore also argued that the CISG is the basis for determining the validity of the contract; under the CISG, the contract was validly formed and effective, and even if Chinese law applied, the contract should be found valid and effective.

This Court holds:

I. Issues concerning the applicable law and the validity of the contract

This case involves a dispute over an international sales contract; both parties are foreign companies, giving the case a foreign element. Article 2 of the Interpretation of the Supreme People's Court on Several Issues Concerning the Application of the Law of the People's Republic of China on the Application of Laws to Foreign-Related Civil Relations (I) provides: "For foreign-related civil relations that arose before the implementation of the Law of the People's Republic of China on the Application of Laws to Foreign-Related Civil Relations, the people's court shall determine the applicable law in accordance with the relevant legal provisions in effect at the time such foreign-related civil relations arose; if there were no provisions at that time, the provisions of the Law on the Application of Laws to Foreign-Related Civil Relations may be applied by reference." The subject Procurement Contract was signed on April 11, 2008, before the implementation of the Law on the Application of Laws to Foreign-Related Civil Relations. Article 145 of the General Principles of the Civil Law of the People's Republic of China in effect at the time the parties signed the Procurement Contract provided: "The parties to a contract involving foreign interests may choose the law applicable to the settlement of their contractual disputes, unless otherwise provided by law. If the parties to a contract involving foreign interests have not made a choice, the law of the country that has the closest connection with the contract shall apply." The parties in this case agreed in the contract that it should be made, governed, and interpreted in accordance with the laws in effect in the State of New York, USA at the time. This agreement does not violate the law and should be found valid. Since Singapore and Germany, the countries where the parties' places of business are located, are both Contracting States to the CISG, and the United States is also a Contracting State, and during the first-instance proceedings both parties consistently chose to apply the CISG as the basis for determining their rights and obligations, without excluding the application of the CISG, the Jiangsu High People's Court correctly applied the CISG in hearing this case. For issues arising in the case that are not covered by the CISG, the law of the State of New York chosen by the parties should apply. The "Digest of Case Law on the United Nations Convention on Contracts for the International Sale of Goods" is not part of the CISG and cannot serve as the legal basis for adjudicating this case. However, it may be used as an appropriate reference material for accurately understanding the meaning of the relevant provisions of the Convention.

When hearing a contract dispute, the people's court must first determine the validity of the contract, regardless of whether the parties dispute it. Article 4 of the CISG provides: "This Convention governs only the formation of the contract of sale and the rights and obligations of the seller and the buyer arising from such a contract. In particular, except as otherwise expressly provided in this Convention, it is not concerned with: (a) the validity of the contract or of any of its provisions or of any usage; (b) the effect which the contract may have on the property in the goods sold." Since the Convention does not address the validity of the contract, this issue must be determined under the law of the State of New York chosen by the parties. Krupp submitted the Uniform Commercial Code and relevant case law during the second instance, arguing that the contract should be found valid. Although Sinochem Singapore did not recognize the explanation of U.S. law provided by Krupp's agent, it did not object to the U.S. law submitted by Krupp and also argued that the contract should be found valid. This Court confirms the U.S. law submitted by Krupp. According to the U.S. law submitted and confirmed by both parties, the subject Procurement Contract does not contain any circumstances that would render it invalid; therefore, the Procurement Contract is valid.

II. Whether the Jiangsu High People's Court ruled beyond the scope of the claim

One of Sinochem Singapore's claims in the first instance was that Krupp's fundamental breach entitled it to rescind the Procurement Contract between the parties. The CISG does not distinguish between rescission and avoidance in the same way as Chinese law; it provides that where one party commits a fundamental breach, the other party is entitled to declare the contract avoided. "Declaration of avoidance" under the Convention is essentially equivalent to "rescission of contract" under Chinese law. Based on Sinochem Singapore's claim and the facts and reasons it relied on, combined with the relevant provisions of the CISG, the Jiangsu High People's Court considered that Sinochem Singapore's request for the court to rescind the contract should be understood as a request to declare the contract avoided under the CISG, which was consistent with Sinochem Singapore's true intention. Sinochem Singapore also acknowledged this and raised no objection. The Jiangsu High People's Court did not rule beyond the scope of the claim. Krupp's argument that the Jiangsu High People's Court exceeded the scope of the claim is not sustainable.

III. Whether Sinochem Singapore and Sinochem Holding Company had an agency relationship

Sinochem Singapore claimed that its relationship with Sinochem Holding Company was one of consignment, and it provided a reasonable explanation for signing a sales contract with Sinochem Holding Company for customs clearance purposes, submitting the consignment sales contract. Moreover, on October 15, 2008, Sinochem Holding Company communicated with Krupp on behalf of Sinochem Singapore regarding the HGI index of the petroleum coke. Thereafter, Sinochem Singapore itself also communicated with Krupp many times regarding the HGI index, and Krupp never argued that Sinochem Singapore had already resold the petroleum coke to Sinochem Holding Company and thus had no right to raise objections about the HGI index. During the first-instance proceedings, Sinochem Singapore also entrusted Sinochem Holding Company to sell the petroleum coke on its behalf to mitigate losses. The Jiangsu High People's Court, based on this, found that the relationship between Sinochem Singapore and Sinochem Holding Company was one of consignment sales. It was not improper for the court to decline to support Krupp's argument that the relationship was one of sales and that Sinochem Singapore had already sold the petroleum coke to Sinochem Holding Company at the original contract price and therefore suffered no loss. Krupp's argument that the Jiangsu High People's Court erroneously found an agency relationship between Sinochem Singapore and Sinochem Holding Company is not sustainable.

IV. Whether Krupp committed a fundamental breach

In the Procurement Contract, the parties agreed that the typical HGI index of the petroleum coke would be between 36 and 46. However, the HGI index of the petroleum coke actually delivered by Krupp was 32, lower than the minimum typical HGI index agreed upon, failing to meet the contractual specifications. The Jiangsu High People's Court correctly found that Krupp had committed a breach.

The focal issue in this dispute is whether the aforementioned breach of contract by Krupp Germany constitutes a fundamental breach. First, as to the content of the parties' agreement in the contract regarding the chemical and physical property specifications required for the petroleum coke, the contract set forth seven specifications: moisture content, sulfur content, ash content, volatile matter content, size, calorific value, and hardness (HGI value). Based on the facts as they stand, Sinochem Singapore only raised objections regarding the HGI index of the petroleum coke delivered by Krupp Germany as non-conforming with the contract, and raised no objections concerning the other six specifications. Considering the witness testimony submitted by the parties and the statements made by witnesses during their court appearance, the HGI index represents the grindability index of petroleum coke: the lower the index, the harder the petroleum coke and the more difficult it is to grind. However, as the Jiangsu High People's Court pointed out in its first-instance judgment, even the explanation submitted by Sinochem Singapore's own party, the School of Materials Science and Engineering of Shanghai University, did not deny that petroleum coke with an HGI index of 32 could be used, but only stated that its uses were limited. Therefore, it can be determined that although the HGI index of the petroleum coke in question did not conform to the contract, this batch of petroleum coke still had use value. Second, during the first-instance trial of this case, Sinochem Singapore, in order to reduce losses, actively made efforts to resell the petroleum coke in question. In its correspondence to Krupp Germany on related issues, it explicitly stated that the resale price of this batch of petroleum coke was "not lower than the reasonable market price." This fact demonstrates that the petroleum coke in question could be sold at a reasonable price. Third, comprehensively considering the understanding of the provisions on fundamental breach in the CISG by the courts of other countries, where a buyer can use or resell the goods, even at a discount, without unreasonable inconvenience, the non-conformity in quality still does not constitute a fundamental breach. Therefore, this Court holds that Krupp Germany's delivery of petroleum coke with an HGI index of 32 does not constitute a fundamental breach. The Jiangsu High People's Court's determination that Krupp Germany's conduct constituted a fundamental breach and its judgment declaring the Procurement Contract void were errors in the application of law, and this Court hereby corrects them. Krupp Germany's ground of appeal on the issue of whether it constituted a fundamental breach is meritorious, and this Court sustains it.

Given that Krupp Germany's conduct does not constitute a fundamental breach, Sinochem Singapore is not entitled to declare the contract void on that basis. Consequently, Krupp Germany's appeal argument concerning whether Sinochem Singapore made a notice of avoidance of the contract on the ground of fundamental breach within a reasonable time need not be further reviewed, and this Court renders no judgment on this issue.

V. Liability of the Parties

Although Krupp Germany's delivery of petroleum coke with an HGI index not conforming to the contract does not constitute a fundamental breach, as discussed above, because the delivered goods did not conform to the contract, the Jiangsu High People's Court's finding of breach of contract was correct. According to the terms of the Procurement Contract, if Sinochem Singapore discovered that the quality or quantity of the petroleum coke did not conform to the quality or quantity determined at the port of loading, it was entitled to file a claim against Krupp Germany within 60 days from the date the petroleum coke arrived at the port of destination. In this case, the goods arrived at Nanjing Port on September 8, 2008. On October 15, 2008, Sinochem Holding Company sent a letter to Krupp Germany, stating that the HGI index of the delivered petroleum coke seriously deviated from the range stipulated in the contract, that the downstream users could not use it and refused to accept the goods, that the situation was serious, and requesting Krupp Germany to provide a solution as soon as possible. During its defense at the first-instance trial, Krupp Germany acknowledged that Sinochem Holding Company's conduct represented Sinochem Singapore. On November 4, 2008, Sinochem Singapore again sent a letter to Krupp Germany, stating that the HGI index of the petroleum coke delivered by Krupp Germany seriously deviated from the range stipulated in the contract, constituting a material breach, and requesting Krupp Germany to handle the matter properly. The above facts demonstrate that Sinochem Singapore raised objections to the quality of the goods and asserted its relevant rights within the time limit stipulated in the contract. Therefore, Krupp Germany's ground of appeal that Sinochem Singapore failed to raise a quality objection within a reasonable time and therefore lost its right to claim non-conformity cannot stand, and this Court does not sustain it.

The HGI index of the petroleum coke delivered by Krupp Germany did not conform to the contract, objectively causing Sinochem Singapore to be unable to resell it promptly. Although Sinochem Singapore managed to resell it through efforts, it suffered losses due to market price fluctuations. Therefore, Krupp Germany shall bear corresponding liability for damages for the price differential loss of USD 2,684,302.9 and interest, as well as the storage fee loss of USD 164,071.31. The occurrence of these losses also involved market risk factors, so Sinochem Singapore shall also bear the corresponding losses itself. Taxes, fees, and lump-sum charges are expenses that Sinochem Singapore should bear during the performance of the contract. Where its request to declare the contract void cannot be sustained, Sinochem Singapore shall bear the taxes, fees, and lump-sum charges itself.

In summary, the facts found in the first-instance judgment of the Jiangsu High People's Court are generally clear, but there are errors in the application of certain laws and improper determination of liability. This Court hereby corrects them. Pursuant to Article 145 of the General Principles of the Civil Law of the PRC, Articles 1, 4, 25, 39, 49, 74, and 78 of the United Nations Convention on Contracts for the International Sale of Goods, Article 170, Paragraph 1, Item (2) of the Civil Procedure Law of the PRC, and Article 2 of the Interpretation (I) of the Supreme People's Court on Several Issues concerning the Application of the Law of the PRC on the Laws Applicable to Foreign-Related Civil Relations, the judgment is as follows:

1. Set aside Item 1 of the civil judgment (2009) Su Min San Chu Zi No. 0004 of the Jiangsu High People's Court.

2. Amend Item 2 of the civil judgment (2009) Su Min San Chu Zi No. 0004 of the Jiangsu High People's Court to: ThyssenKrupp Metallurgical Products Co., Ltd. shall, within thirty days from the effective date of this judgment, compensate Sinochem International (Singapore) Co., Ltd. for the loss of the price of the goods in the amount of USD 1,610,581.74, and pay interest thereon from September 25, 2008 to the date of payment determined by this judgment (calculated at the USD lending rate of the Bank of China for the corresponding period).

3. Amend Item 3 of the civil judgment (2009) Su Min San Chu Zi No. 0004 of the Jiangsu High People's Court to: ThyssenKrupp Metallurgical Products Co., Ltd. shall, within thirty days from the effective date of this judgment, compensate Sinochem International (Singapore) Co., Ltd. for the storage fee loss in the amount of USD 98,442.79.

4. Dismiss the other claims of Sinochem International (Singapore) Co., Ltd.

If the payment obligation is not performed within the period specified in this judgment, the debt for the delayed performance shall be doubled in accordance with Article 253 of the Civil Procedure Law of the PRC.

The first-instance case acceptance fee of RMB 306,432 shall be borne by ThyssenKrupp Metallurgical Products Co., Ltd. in the amount of RMB 183,859.2 and by Sinochem International (Singapore) Co., Ltd. in the amount of RMB 122,572.8. The second-instance case acceptance fee of RMB 306,432 shall be borne by ThyssenKrupp Metallurgical Products Co., Ltd. in the amount of RMB 183,859.2 and by Sinochem International (Singapore) Co., Ltd. in the amount of RMB 122,572.8.

This judgment is final.

Presiding Judge: Ren Xuefeng
Acting Judge: Cheng Mingzhu
Acting Judge: Zhu Ke
